title: Last year’s video I was referencing:@Joe Weinberg #broadway #theatre
transcript: Let's talk about Scott Rudin again, shall we? I made a similar video to this last summer, but let's revisit now that he's had his first season back and his next season at least partly announced. I approached last year's video by examining his artistic reputation, the praise he's gotten as a curator of good taste. And I did that, as I said, not to pull focus from the alleged employee abuse, but because it's that reputation that not only kept him in power for so long, but has now allowed him to be welcomed back with open arms. It's become quite clear that his long standing target demographic, the sort of cultured New York Liberal elite, don't care about the allegations against him. Many of them maybe don't know, but those that do know, don't care. Or they give him the benefit of the doubt that he's changed, probably without asking anyone who has worked under him recently. And probably his target demo is mostly not on TikTok, which kind of puts us in a tricky position as far as trying to speak out about this. But I think when these conversations do take place with his target demo, some focus does have to be on the work, because that's the framework they are using to decide that Scott Rudin still belongs in the industry. So I would ask them to interrogate honestly: what does Scott Rudin bring to the industry that other producers don't or that we can't do without? I posited in my video from last year that the branding of classy prestige that he's managed to cultivate around his work might have been doing more heavy lifting than most of us want to admit. Not to say that he hasn't done a lot of great work. I think I would be losing credibility in this argument if I tried to pretend that wasn't the case. But it was far from the Midas touch, both in terms of quality and commercial success. Like any Broadway producer, his programming was a mixed bag. And I'd argue that has more or less continued to be the case, although, I admit, it’s subjective. And it's a small sample size from this past season. I do think Desth of a Salesman benefited considerably from the fact that it was an unusually weak season on Broadway, which kind of fed into the perception that Rudin is offering something that no one else can offer. And I'll get more into that mindset in a second. But looking now to this week's announcement, I think we're seeing something from him that we didn't even see before. The whole “thing” with Scott Rudin was that he was this bold and imaginative curator, unafraid to take risks. But this new announcement feels like he's doing what everyone else is doing. I've been on the record many times that I am more in favor of celebrity casting than not. more than most, maybe. But even for me, there's something kind of tacky about this Small Mouth Sounds cast with this hodgepodge of names that feels like it came from a random celebrity Generator. Dare I say there's even a whiff of desperation about it, which is not something you expect from the great purveyor of taste. Downstate is more in line with what he's known for - Kind of, in the sense that it is genuinely a very boundary-pushing play that you wouldn't expect to see on Broadway. But again, he's doing what a lot of producers are doing right now. Not necessarily shepherding these plays to fruition, but pulling them off the shelf 5-10 years after they already proved themselves as a hit off Broadway. He's not even the only producer doing that with a hot-button boundary-pushing play this season. We also have Gloria coming to Broadway. So again, to his target demo: is this really the imagination, risk taking and the unparalleled eye for taste that made Scott Rudin's return feel “worth it” to you? And at the risk of going off the rails here, I also think this comes back to the kind of Broadway supremacy mindset. All these Broadway producers, if they're not reviving well worn classics, are magnanimously plucking from the semi-recent canon of off-Broadway hits. But the play that's going to be *that* in 5-10 years is probably one that you can see premiere in New York off Broadway this season. My point being that putting Broadway on a pedestal facilitates putting people like Scott Rudin on a pedestal for being brave enough to bring these shows to Broadway. Okay, I know I've been rambling a little bit, so to kind of summarize the core things I'm trying to say here: 1. As I said in my video last year, I don't think Scott Rudin's artistic track record is that far above average. 2. His newest upcoming Cash Cow isn't even really in the vein of what people like about his programming. And 3, even when his work is very good, I invite you to consider whether we really need it more than we need a world without people like Scott Rudin in power. Especially when good theater was and still is being produced elsewhere in New York, if you care to look for it.
classificationReason: Industry commentary about producer Scott Rudin's return to Broadway and the debate around his alleged employee abuse; no specific production is reviewed and no first-hand stage attendance is described.
